Monday. Chaitanya taped chart paper to the classroom wall. "Farewell theme. Every idea goes up, even silly ones. Nobody says 'that won't work' until Wednesday." Farhan snorted but wrote "Space Station". By the last bell the sheet held thirty ideas, from "Old Film Posters" to "Board Games Night".

Wednesday. The committee circled back. "If we argue about thirty, we'll fight till March," Chaitanya said aloud. "Let's keep only what fits the hall and our budget." Talk trimmed the list to three: Retro Radio, Monsoon Fair, and Space Station. Twelve hands voted on slips folded into a lunchbox.

Friday. Monsoon Fair won by two votes. Farhan, whose idea lost, shrugged and offered to paint paper boats. "At least I got my rocket on the wall first," he said, grinning.

qa.a: By the last bell on Monday the sheet held thirty ideas.

Sit, Vijay, you're making the chai go cold. You asked how your Asif chacha ever organised anything. Well, I was fifteen, and our school wanted a Founders' Day stall. Six of us, and everyone had a favourite idea and a loud voice. First meeting was pure shouting.

We filled the blackboard: a puppet show, a pickle sale, a quiz, a mehendi corner, even a snake charmer, which was mine. Then we talked, rubbed out what cost too much, and kept three. We voted with pebbles in a steel tumbler.

The quiz won. My snake charmer lost badly, and I sulked for an hour. But I ran the scoreboard, and nobody could say they hadn't been heard.

"Four jobs, four names, four dates," he told the group. "Decoration: Samir, sample colours by Tuesday. Music: me, playlist to Ma'am by Thursday. Food: Leela and Joshua, final list Wednesday. Invites: Parveen, cards in every class by Monday."

Samir frowned. "Last year we just said 'everyone helps'."

"And last year nobody bought plates, because everybody thought somebody else had." Hemant tapped the sheet. "If your date slips, you tell me that same day. No shame, we just fix it."

On Tuesday Samir showed up with swatches. On Wednesday the food list was short by juice, and Leela added it before lunch. The party wasn't perfect, but every job had someone.

14 Feb, night

Worst Valentine's-week social ever, and it's mostly my fault. Pema kept asking last week, "Joseph, did you book the speaker? The chairs?" I kept saying chill, the hall has stuff, we'll sort it on the day.

Today we reached at four. The hall speaker crackled and died after one song. The caretaker said the good chairs were locked for a PTA meeting, so forty people stood or sat on the floor. Pema ran to her aunt's house for a phone speaker. It was so quiet you could hear people chewing.

Some juniors left before the games. One girl said "this is it?" and I pretended not to hear.

I feel like an idiot. Pema didn't even say I told you so, which somehow made it worse. Tomorrow I'm apologising properly.

qa.a: The caretaker said the good chairs were locked for a PTA meeting.

qa.a: Joseph feels embarrassed and guilty, calling himself an idiot and noting that Pema's silence made it worse.

qa.a: Pema was likely frustrated and let down, since the warnings were ignored and she ended up running for a spare speaker.

Vaibhav, you want to know why your Hafsa nani always keeps an umbrella in the car? Let me tell you about my school's annual day, back when I was sixteen.

Our headmistress made the organising committee sit in her office. "Close your eyes. It's the evening after annual day, and it failed. Tell me why." We felt silly. Then answers came. "The generator won't start." "It rains and the shamiana leaks." "Half the dancers get chickenpox."

She made us write a fix beside each fear. We borrowed a second generator from the mosque committee. We tied plastic sheets over the shamiana. Every dance had two understudies.

It rained that evening, and the first generator coughed and stopped. We lit the stage with the second one while parents clapped, never knowing. I've planned that way ever since.

qa.a: They borrowed a second generator from the mosque committee.

qa.a: Writing a fix beside each fear mattered most, because only the second generator and the plastic sheets turned worried guesses into real protection on the night.

qa.q: How might the headmistress have felt watching the stage lights come back?
qa.a: The headmistress probably felt quietly satisfied and relieved, seeing the exercise she insisted on save the evening.

Sonali beta, you're asking me how to plan your class picnic? Then listen to your Bhupen mama's story first.

When I was seventeen in Guwahati, a few of us wanted a riverside Bihu party for our class. My first idea was: go at night, tell nobody, bring a big speaker. My friend's father heard and just asked, "And if someone slips into the river in the dark?" I had no answer.

So we did it properly. Our class teacher agreed and came along. Every parent signed a slip. We fixed the end at six, before dark. We picked the flat bank near the ghat where the boatmen could see us, kept everyone away from the deep side, and arranged two autos to drop the girls home in groups.

It felt less wild. But every single person got home safe.

The farewell party for Class 12 had one problem nobody had budgeted for: the only free venue, the school terrace, closed at dusk and had a low parapet.

Neelam, head of the organising group, sat with Usha in the empty classroom, the power cut making the fan still. They had three days and almost no money.

"We can't just sneak up there after dark," Neelam said, rubbing her eyes. Usha nodded and started a list by candlelight.

They asked the vice-principal, who agreed to a four-to-seven slot if two teachers stayed. They marked a chalk line two metres from the parapet and assigned volunteers to watch it. Parents got a message with the end time. For the few who lived far, Usha matched them with classmates' families driving the same way.

Dear Vasudha,

I owe you an apology, and a confession about the Children's Day fair.

You were right. I redid the stall layout six times. Every night I rewrote the timetable, then sent it to all nine volunteers at 11 pm with "small changes!!" By the second week, only four people were replying. By the final week, two.

Dear Lavanya,

You'll laugh, but I finally understood what Miss Kurian meant about buffers.

Our Science Day assembly was supposed to open with a talk by a scientist from the university. At 9:00 she messaged: bus broke down, reaching by 9:45. I had 300 students on the ground and nothing planned for forty-five minutes.

My brain froze for about ten seconds. Then I grabbed the quiz team and asked them to start early. After the quiz I moved the model display forward and let kids walk around it. By the time the scientist arrived, people were still excited.

At our review, Aman said we should always keep fifteen spare minutes and one filler item ready. He's right. I'd been so proud of a tight timetable that I forgot tight means fragile.

Write soon,
Trisha

"Your speech says 'I will bring change'," Manoj said, reading Chinmay's draft on the canteen bench. "Change to what?"

"Everything. The school needs it."

"Everyone says that. Did you ask anyone what they want?"

Chinmay was quiet. Then: "Okay. Let's ask."

"The canteen line," said a Class 8 girl. "Twenty minutes, then the bell."

"No footballs that aren't flat," said a boy.

"Library shuts at two," said someone from Class 12. "We have free periods at three."

Back on the bench, Chinmay crossed out 'change'. "So it's three things. Two canteen counters at break. Pump and replace footballs each term. Ask if the library can stay open till four." He looked up. "These I can actually argue for."

Manoj grinned. "Now it sounds like you listened."

When I decided to run for school captain last year, my first poster said, "A Better Tomorrow." Nikita, my friend from the hostel, looked at it and asked, "Better how?" I didn't have an answer, and that bothered me all night.

So I made a small notebook and spent a week asking people one question at dinner and in the corridors: what's hard here? I thought I'd hear big things. Instead I heard about the hostel water cooler that leaked, the football nets full of holes, and the reading room that closed before prep time ended.

That's when it clicked for me. Voters don't live in "tomorrow". They live in queues and broken nets.

I rewrote everything around those three fixes. I'm Siddharth, and I didn't win by much, but I won, and I remember that notebook.

qa.a: The first poster said, "A Better Tomorrow."

qa.q: What else could Siddharth have done besides the notebook?
qa.a: Siddharth could have held a short open meeting in the hostel common room, so students could build on each other's complaints and rank them.

qa.q: How might Nikita see the change in the campaign?
qa.a: Nikita would probably feel pleased and a bit proud, since one honest question pushed the campaign toward real problems.

subtype: Approach: building a small campaign team [Action]
passage:
I'm Reena, and I thought running for house captain meant giving one good speech. My friend Dhruv laughed when I said that. "You'll talk to your own class. What about the other four hundred?"

So I built a team. Dhruv took posters, because he could draw. A girl from Class 8 who played basketball with me offered to visit junior classes. A Class 11 boy from my coding club helped me write a short speech. There were four of us.

We met for ten minutes every morning before assembly, on the steps outside the lab. Each person said what they'd done and what was blocked. Once the posters were torn down in one corridor; the next morning we'd already replaced them.

I lost narrowly. But juniors I'd never met told me they voted for me, and that surprised me more than anything.

qa.q: Where did the team meet every morning?
qa.a: They met on the steps outside the lab for ten minutes every morning before assembly.

qa.q: How did Reena feel when juniors said they had voted for Reena?
qa.a: Reena felt surprised and quietly touched, since those were students Reena had never met.

qa.q: What else could Reena's team have done to reach more voters?
qa.a: They could have asked each class what it most wanted and shaped a line of the speech for each group, not just visited them.

qa.q: How might Dhruv see Reena's change of plan after his comment?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt pleased and respected, since Reena took his warning seriously and gave him the posters to run.

grounding: A reflective account of a candidate recruiting helpers from different classes for posters, visits and speeches, and meeting briefly each day to check progress.
